lessons.title: Lesson 1: React Fundamentals & JSX
lessons.html:
React Introduction & JSX

React builds UIs using components. JSX lets you write HTML in JavaScript.

JSX Basics:

const name = 'Alice';
const element = <h1>Hello, {name}!</h1>;

First Component:

function Welcome() {
  return (
    <div>
      <h1>Welcome to React</h1>
      <p>Start building amazing UIs!</p>
    </div>
  );
}

Setup: npx create-react-app my-app

lessons.title: Lesson 3: State & useState Hook
lessons.html:
Managing Component State

useState adds state to functional components. Triggers re-render on change.

Counter Example:

import { useState } from 'react';

function Counter() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);

  return (
    <div>
      <p>Count: {count}</p>
      <button onClick={() => setCount(count + 1)}>+</button>
      <button onClick={() => setCount(count - 1)}>-</button>
    </div>
  );
}

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Event Handling

React Event System

React events use camelCase. Event handlers are functions.

Todo Input Form:

function TodoForm() {
  const [text, setText] = useState('');

  const handleSubmit = (e) => {
    e.preventDefault();
    if (text.trim()) {
      addTodo(text);
      setText('');
    }
  };

  return (
    <form onSubmit={handleSubmit}>
      <input 
        value={text}
        onChange={(e) => setText(e.target.value)}
        placeholder="Add todo..."
      />
    </form>

}

lessons.title: Lesson 6: useEffect Hook
lessons.html:
Side Effects in React

useEffect handles API calls, subscriptions, DOM manipulation.

Fetch Data:

import { useState, useEffect } from 'react';

function UserProfile({ userId }) {
  const [user, setUser] = useState(null);

  useEffect(() => {
    fetch(`/api/users/${userId}`)
      .then(res => res.json())
      .then(setUser);
  }, [userId]);  // Runs when userId changes

  if (!user) return <div>Loading...</div>;
  return <h1>{user.name}</h1>;
}

lessons.title: Lesson 8: React Router & Navigation
lessons.html:
Client-Side Routing with React Router

React Router enables navigation between views without page reloads. It's the standard routing library for React.

Router Setup:

import { BrowserRouter, Routes, Route, Link, useParams } from 'react-router-dom';

function App() {
  return (
    <BrowserRouter>
      <nav>
        <Link to="/">Home</Link>
        <Link to="/about">About</Link>
        <Link to="/users">Users</Link>
      </nav>

      <Routes>
        <Route path="/" element={<Home />} />
        <Route path="/about" element={<About />} />
        <Route path="/users" element={<UsersList />} />
        <Route path="/users/:id" element={<UserProfile />} />
        <Route path="*" element={<NotFound />} />
      </Routes>
    </BrowserRouter>
  );
}

function UserProfile() {
  const { id } = useParams();
  return <h1>User Profile: {id}</h1>;
}

Nested Routes & Layouts:

import { Outlet, NavLink } from 'react-router-dom';

function DashboardLayout() {
  return (
    <div className="dashboard">
      <aside>
        <NavLink to="profile">Profile</NavLink>
        <NavLink to="settings">Settings</NavLink>
      </aside>
      <main>
        <Outlet />  {/* Child routes render here */}
      </main>
    </div>
  );
}

// Usage:
<Route path="dashboard" element={<DashboardLayout />}>
  <Route index element={<DashboardHome />} />
  <Route path="profile" element={<Profile />} />
  <Route path="settings" element={<Settings />} />
</Route>

Practice Exercises:

  1. Build a multi-page app with 5+ routes and navigation
  2. Add protected routes that redirect to login
  3. Implement breadcrumb navigation from routes

Key Takeaways:

  • Routes map URLs to components
  • useParams extracts dynamic segments from URLs
  • Outlet renders nested child routes

lessons.title: Lesson 9: Forms & Formik
lessons.html:
Form Management with Formik

Formik simplifies form state, validation, and submission in React. It reduces boilerplate significantly.

Formik Basics:

import { Formik, Form, Field, ErrorMessage } from 'formik';
import * as Yup from 'yup';

const validationSchema = Yup.object({
  name: Yup.string()
    .min(2, 'Must be 2+ characters')
    .required('Required'),
  email: Yup.string()
    .email('Invalid email address')
    .required('Required'),
  age: Yup.number()
    .min(18, 'Must be 18+')
    .max(120, 'Invalid age')
    .required('Required'),
});

function RegistrationForm() {
  return (
    <Formik
      initialValues={{ name: '', email: '', age: '' }}
      validationSchema={validationSchema}
      onSubmit={(values, { setSubmitting }) => {
        setTimeout(() => {
          alert(JSON.stringify(values, null, 2));
          setSubmitting(false);
        }, 400);
      }}
    >
      {({ isSubmitting }) => (
        <Form>
          <Field type="text" name="name" placeholder="Name" />
          <ErrorMessage name="name" component="div" className="error" />

          <Field type="email" name="email" placeholder="Email" />
          <ErrorMessage name="email" component="div" className="error" />

          <Field type="number" name="age" placeholder="Age" />
          <ErrorMessage name="age" component="div" className="error" />

          <button type="submit" disabled={isSubmitting}>
            Submit
          </button>
        </Form>
      )}
    </Formik>
  );
}

Practice Exercises:

  1. Create a multi-step registration form
  2. Add custom validation for password strength
  3. Implement a dynamic form with add/remove fields

Key Takeaways:

  • Formik manages form state and validation
  • Yup provides declarative validation schemas
  • Field and ErrorMessage components render form elements

lessons.title: Lesson 10: State Management with Context API
lessons.html:
Global State with Context

React Context provides a way to share state across the component tree without prop drilling.

Auth Context:

import { createContext, useContext, useState, useEffect } from 'react';

const AuthContext = createContext(null);

export function AuthProvider({ children }) {
  const [user, setUser] = useState(null);
  const [loading, setLoading] = useState(true);

  useEffect(() => {
    // Check for existing session
    const token = localStorage.getItem('token');
    if (token) {
      fetchUser(token).then(user => {
        setUser(user);
        setLoading(false);
      });
    } else {
      setLoading(false);
    }
  }, []);

  const login = async (email, password) => {
    const { token, user } = await api.login(email, password);
    localStorage.setItem('token', token);
    setUser(user);
    return user;
  };

  const logout = () => {
    localStorage.removeItem('token');
    setUser(null);
  };

  return (
    <AuthContext.Provider value={{ user, loading, login, logout }}>
      {children}
    </AuthContext.Provider>
  );
}

export function useAuth() {
  const context = useContext(AuthContext);
  if (!context) {
    throw new Error('useAuth must be used within AuthProvider');
  }
  return context;
}

Using the Context:

function Profile() {
  const { user, logout } = useAuth();

  if (!user) return <Navigate to="/login" />;

  return (
    <div>
      <h1>Welcome, {user.name}!</h1>
      <button onClick={logout}>Logout</button>
    </div>
  );
}

Practice Exercises:

  1. Create a ThemeContext with dark/light mode toggle
  2. Build a CartContext for an e-commerce app
  3. Add a NotificationContext for global alerts

Key Takeaways:

  • Context eliminates prop drilling
  • Provider wraps the component tree
  • Custom hooks provide clean consumer API

lessons.title: Lesson 11: State Management with Redux Toolkit
lessons.html:
Global State with Redux

Redux Toolkit simplifies Redux with less boilerplate. It's the standard for large-scale React apps.

Redux Slice:

import { createSlice, configureStore } from '@reduxjs/toolkit';

const counterSlice = createSlice({
  name: 'counter',
  initialState: { value: 0, status: 'idle' },
  reducers: {
    increment: (state) => {
      state.value += 1;
    },
    decrement: (state) => {
      state.value -= 1;
    },
    incrementByAmount: (state, action) => {
      state.value += action.payload;
    },
  },
});

export const { increment, decrement, incrementByAmount } = counterSlice.actions;
export default counterSlice.reducer;

// Store setup
const store = configureStore({
  reducer: {
    counter: counterReducer,
    users: usersReducer,
  },
});

Using Redux in Components:

import { useSelector, useDispatch } from 'react-redux';
import { increment, decrement } from './counterSlice';

function Counter() {
  const count = useSelector((state) => state.counter.value);
  const dispatch = useDispatch();

  return (
    <div>
      <h1>Count: {count}</h1>
      <button onClick={() => dispatch(increment())}>+</button>
      <button onClick={() => dispatch(decrement())}>-</button>
    </div>
  );
}

Async Thunks:

import { createAsyncThunk } from '@reduxjs/toolkit';

export const fetchUsers = createAsyncThunk(
  'users/fetchUsers',
  async (_, { rejectWithValue }) => {
    try {
      const response = await fetch('/api/users');
      return await response.json();
    } catch (err) {
      return rejectWithValue(err.message);
    }
  }
);

Practice Exercises:

  1. Set up Redux for a todo app with async API calls
  2. Create slices for users, posts, and comments
  3. Add loading states and error handling to async thunks

Key Takeaways:

  • Redux Toolkit reduces boilerplate vs classic Redux
  • createAsyncThunk handles async API calls
  • Immer enables mutable state syntax in reducers

lessons.title: Lesson 12: Testing with React Testing Library
lessons.html:
Component Testing

React Testing Library encourages testing components from the user's perspective.

Component Tests:

import { render, screen, fireEvent } from '@testing-library/react';
import userEvent from '@testing-library/user-event';
import { Counter } from './Counter';

describe('Counter', () => {
  test('renders initial count', () => {
    render(<Counter />);
    expect(screen.getByText('Count: 0')).toBeInTheDocument();
  });

  test('increments count on click', async () => {
    const user = userEvent.setup();
    render(<Counter />);

    await user.click(screen.getByText('+'));
    expect(screen.getByText('Count: 1')).toBeInTheDocument();
  });

  test('handles multiple clicks', async () => {
    const user = userEvent.setup();
    render(<Counter />);

    await user.click(screen.getByText('+'));
    await user.click(screen.getByText('+'));
    await user.click(screen.getByText('+'));
    expect(screen.getByText('Count: 3')).toBeInTheDocument();
  });
});

Async Test with API:

import { rest } from 'msw';
import { setupServer } from 'msw/node';

const server = setupServer(
  rest.get('/api/users', (req, res, ctx) => {
    return res(ctx.json([
      { id: 1, name: 'Alice' },
      { id: 2, name: 'Bob' },
    ]));
  })
);

beforeAll(() => server.listen());
afterEach(() => server.resetHandlers());
afterAll(() => server.close());

test('fetches and displays users', async () => {
  render(<UserList />);
  expect(await screen.findByText('Alice')).toBeInTheDocument();
  expect(await screen.findByText('Bob')).toBeInTheDocument();
});

Practice Exercises:

  1. Write tests for a form with validation
  2. Mock API calls with MSW for integration tests
  3. Test context providers and custom hooks

Key Takeaways:

  • Test user interactions, not implementation details
  • screen queries find elements by accessibility
  • MSW mocks HTTP requests at the network level

lessons.title: Lesson 13: Custom Hooks
lessons.html:
Reusable Logic with Custom Hooks

Custom hooks extract reusable stateful logic from components, keeping code DRY.

Common Hooks:

import { useState, useEffect, useCallback, useRef } from 'react';

// useLocalStorage
export function useLocalStorage(key, initialValue) {
  const [storedValue, setStoredValue] = useState(() => {
    try {
      const item = window.localStorage.getItem(key);
      return item ? JSON.parse(item) : initialValue;
    } catch (error) {
      console.error(error);
      return initialValue;
    }
  });

  const setValue = (value) => {
    try {
      const valueToStore = value instanceof Function ? value(storedValue) : value;
      setStoredValue(valueToStore);
      window.localStorage.setItem(key, JSON.stringify(valueToStore));
    } catch (error) {
      console.error(error);
    }
  };

  return [storedValue, setValue];
}

// useDebounce
export function useDebounce(value, delay = 500) {
  const [debouncedValue, setDebouncedValue] = useState(value);

  useEffect(() => {
    const timer = setTimeout(() => setDebouncedValue(value), delay);
    return () => clearTimeout(timer);
  }, [value, delay]);

  return debouncedValue;
}

// useFetch
export function useFetch(url) {
  const [data, setData] = useState(null);
  const [loading, setLoading] = useState(true);
  const [error, setError] = useState(null);

  useEffect(() => {
    let cancelled = false;
    setLoading(true);

    fetch(url)
      .then(res => res.json())
      .then(data => {
        if (!cancelled) {
          setData(data);
          setLoading(false);
        }
      })
      .catch(err => {
        if (!cancelled) {
          setError(err);
          setLoading(false);
        }
      });

    return () => { cancelled = true; };
  }, [url]);

  return { data, loading, error };
}

Practice Exercises:

  1. Create a useMediaQuery hook for responsive design
  2. Build a useEventListener hook for DOM events
  3. Implement useIntersectionObserver for lazy loading

Key Takeaways:

  • Custom hooks start with the word 'use'
  • Hooks can use other hooks internally
  • Hooks are the primary way to share stateful logic

lessons.title: Lesson 14: Performance Optimization
lessons.html:
React Performance Techniques

React provides tools to avoid unnecessary re-renders and optimize rendering performance.

Memoization:

import { memo, useMemo, useCallback } from 'react';

// Prevent re-render when props haven't changed
const ExpensiveComponent = memo(function ExpensiveComponent({ data, onItemClick }) {
  console.log('Rendering expensive component');
  return (
    <ul>
      {data.map(item => (
        <li key={item.id} onClick={() => onItemClick(item.id)}>
          {item.name}
        </li>
      ))}
    </ul>
  );
});

function Parent() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
  const [items, setItems] = useState(generateLargeArray());

  // Only recompute when items change
  const processedData = useMemo(() => {
    return items.map(item => ({
      ...item,
      processed: expensiveCalculation(item),
    }));
  }, [items]);

  // Stable callback reference
  const handleClick = useCallback((id) => {
    console.log('Clicked:', id);
  }, []);

  return (
    <div>
      <p>Count: {count}</p>
      <button onClick={() => setCount(c => c + 1)}>Re-render parent</button>
      <ExpensiveComponent data={processedData} onItemClick={handleClick} />
    </div>
  );
}

React.lazy & Suspense:

import { lazy, Suspense } from 'react';

const HeavyDashboard = lazy(() => import('./HeavyDashboard'));
const UserProfile = lazy(() => import('./UserProfile'));

function App() {
  return (
    <Suspense fallback={<div className="spinner">Loading...</div>}>
      <Routes>
        <Route path="/dashboard" element={<HeavyDashboard />} />
        <Route path="/users/:id" element={<UserProfile />} />
      </Routes>
    </Suspense>
  );
}

Practice Exercises:

  1. Profile your app with React DevTools Profiler
  2. Add code splitting to a large application
  3. Use virtualization with react-window for long lists

Key Takeaways:

  • memo prevents useless re-renders
  • useMemo caches expensive computations
  • React.lazy enables code splitting

lessons.title: Lesson 15: Next.js & SSR
lessons.html:
Server-Side Rendering with Next.js

Next.js adds server-side rendering, static generation, and API routes to React.

Pages & Routing:

// pages/index.js - SSG (Static Site Generation)
export default function Home({ posts }) {
  return (
    <div>
      <h1>Blog Posts</h1>
      {posts.map(post => (
        <article key={post.id}>
          <h2>{post.title}</h2>
          <p>{post.excerpt}</p>
        </article>
      ))}
    </div>
  );
}

export async function getStaticProps() {
  const res = await fetch('https://api.example.com/posts');
  const posts = await res.json();

  return {
    props: { posts },
    revalidate: 60,  // ISR: regenerate every 60 seconds
  };
}

// pages/users/[id].js - SSR (Server-Side Rendering)
export default function UserPage({ user }) {
  return <h1>{user.name}</h1>;
}

export async function getServerSideProps({ params }) {
  const res = await fetch(`https://api.example.com/users/${params.id}`);
  const user = await res.json();

  return { props: { user } };
}

API Routes:

// pages/api/users.js
export default function handler(req, res) {
  if (req.method === 'GET') {
    res.status(200).json({ users: [...] });
  } else if (req.method === 'POST') {
    const { name, email } = req.body;
    const newUser = { id: Date.now(), name, email };
    res.status(201).json(newUser);
  } else {
    res.setHeader('Allow', ['GET', 'POST']);
    res.status(405).end(`Method ${req.method} Not Allowed`);
  }
}

Practice Exercises:

  1. Create a Next.js app with SSG and SSR pages
  2. Add API routes for CRUD operations
  3. Implement dynamic routes with getStaticPaths

Key Takeaways:

  • SSG pre-renders pages at build time
  • SSR renders pages on each request
  • ISR combines SSG speed with fresh data
